R04-B-01: Arguments about the legacy of empire often take the form of an account book. On one side of the ledger are the railways, telegraphs, irrigation canals and universities that colonial governments built; on the other are the drained revenues, the famines, the suppressed industries and the humiliations of foreign rule. Defenders of empire add up the first column and find a surplus; its critics add up the second and find a debt. The exchange can continue indefinitely, because each side chooses what to count, and because neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be. The deeper difficulty is that the ledger treats the items in the first column as gifts, things handed over to a population that would otherwise have lacked them. Consider the railway. In much of the colonial world, lines were laid out to connect mines, plantations and cotton-growing districts to the ports, and to move soldiers quickly to places where unrest might break out. Routes, gauges and freight rates were set according to the needs of export trade and military control, and the cost of construction was frequently met from local taxation or guaranteed by it. A railway designed in this way is not a present; it is an investment made by one party, with another party's money, for the first party's purposes. To enter it as a credit in the colonised society's account is to confuse being affected by something with being given it. None of this means that colonial railways were useless to the people who lived alongside them. Passengers, often in numbers that surprised the companies, used the trains to visit distant shrines, to look for work in growing cities, to carry goods to new markets and, eventually, to travel to political meetings that the authorities would have preferred them not to attend. A technology built for one end was turned to others. But this point cuts against the ledger rather than in its favour, since the uses that mattered most to ordinary people were precisely the ones the builders had not intended and could not claim as their contribution. What the account-book approach leaves out, then, is the question of who decided. A society that chooses to borrow money and build a railway, and gets the routes wrong, has made its own mistake and can learn from it. A society that has a railway built for it, on terms set elsewhere, has acquired a piece of infrastructure but not the habit of deciding about infrastructure. That second loss does not appear in any column, which is perhaps why the ledger has proved so durable: it allows both its defenders and its critics to argue about outcomes while ignoring the matter of agency altogether.
R04-B-02: It has become common to say that colonial censuses did not so much count the peoples of the empire as invent them. The enumerator arrived with a schedule of questions and a list of permitted answers, and the population that emerged from the tables, divided into neatly bounded communities of religion, caste, tribe and language, was in this view largely a creation of the administrative imagination. The argument has done valuable work. It has made historians suspicious of treating census categories as simple descriptions of a pre-existing social order, and it has drawn attention to the way in which knowledge and rule were bound together. Yet in its strongest form it claims too much, and in claiming too much it obscures what was genuinely new. The distinctions that census officials recorded were not conjured out of nothing. People in the societies being counted had long spoken of lineage, occupation, locality, sect and status, and had used these terms to arrange marriages, settle disputes and decide whom to eat with. What these older vocabularies did not usually require was that a person belong to exactly one category of each kind, at all times and for all purposes. A weaver might describe himself by his craft in the market, by his lineage at a wedding and by his village when travelling, without feeling that any one of these was his real identity. The census demanded a single answer, written once and then aggregated, and it treated a blank or a double answer as an error to be corrected. The novelty, then, lay less in the categories than in what was done with them. Once fixed and counted, a category could be ranked, compared across districts, and used as the basis for decisions about recruitment, land and, later, political representation. Groups discovered that their recorded size and standing had consequences, and petitions asking to be listed under a different name or placed higher in an official order of precedence became a regular feature of census years. Some observers have treated such petitions as proof that the categories were artificial, mere labels that people manipulated for advantage. But the petitions suggest the opposite conclusion. People do not campaign over labels that mean nothing to them; they campaign over labels that have begun to govern their lives. This is why the categories outlived the governments that produced them. An identity that is only imposed can be thrown off when its author departs. An identity that has been taken up, argued over and attached to rights and resources becomes part of the social world it was once supposed merely to describe. The census, in short, was neither a mirror nor a fiction. It was closer to a mould, into which existing and quite fluid materials were pressed until they set.
R04-B-03: In the decades after the British Empire abolished slavery in the 1830s, sugar planters in colonies such as Mauritius, Trinidad and British Guiana, and later Fiji, turned to a different source of labour: indentured workers, most of them recruited in India, who signed contracts binding them to an estate for a fixed term of years. Ever since, the system has been argued over in terms set by the institution it replaced. Its critics have called it slavery under a new name; its defenders, at the time and since, have insisted that it was a form of voluntary migration, entered into by contract and ended by the contract's expiry. Each side treats the question as one of classification, as though the decisive task were to place indenture on the correct side of the line between slave and free. There are good reasons to resist the first classification. Indentured workers were not property. They could not be sold, their children did not inherit their status, and at the end of the term many returned home, while others stayed, bought land and built communities whose descendants remain in those countries today. To call this slavery is to lose sight of what was specifically terrible about slavery, and it risks erasing the choices, however constrained, that migrants made. But the second classification fares no better. Recruits were often misled about the work and the wages that awaited them; many were illiterate and signed documents they could not read; and once on the estate they found that the contract, far from protecting them, was the instrument of their confinement. This last point is the one that both classifications miss. Colonial labour laws typically made it a criminal offence, not merely a breach of contract, for an indentured worker to be absent from work, to leave the estate without a pass, or to refuse a task. A worker who walked away could be arrested, fined or imprisoned, and the time spent in prison might be added to the term he owed. The coercion, in other words, did not stand outside the contract and contradict it; it was written into the contract and enforced by courts. The language of free agreement and the reality of compulsion were not opposed but fused. Seen this way, indenture is less a halfway house between slavery and freedom than a demonstration that the line between them was never as clean as abolitionists hoped. The abolition of property in persons did not by itself abolish compulsion; it moved compulsion into the law of contract, where it could be presented as the free choice of the person compelled. That is a lesson with uses beyond the nineteenth century. Wherever a worker's right to leave a job is restricted by debt, by the confiscation of documents or by a visa tied to a single employer, the question worth asking is not whether a contract exists, but what the contract permits others to do to the person who signed it.
R04-B-04: When a colony becomes independent, one of the first questions its new government must answer is which language it will govern in. The question is often posed as a choice between authenticity and convenience. On one side stands the language of the former rulers, already established in the courts, the universities and the upper ranks of the civil service, and useful for dealing with the wider world. On the other stand the languages the people actually speak, whose adoption would seem to complete the work of liberation. Put this way, retaining the colonial language looks like a practical compromise with a humiliating past, and abandoning it looks like a costly act of pride. This framing, however, hides the most important feature of the decision, which is that every option distributes advantage and disadvantage among citizens. In a country where many languages are spoken and none is spoken by a clear majority, choosing one of them as the sole language of administration hands a lasting head start to those who grew up speaking it. Their children will sit examinations in their mother tongue while everyone else's children sit them in a second language. Groups that expect to lose from such an arrangement can be relied upon to resist it, sometimes fiercely, and their resistance is not mere sentiment but a reasonable reading of their interests. The colonial language has a curious property in this situation: it is equally foreign to almost everyone. Retaining it therefore spares the state from having to declare one community's speech superior to another's, which is one reason several multilingual states have kept it long after they expected to discard it. But equal foreignness is not equal access. The colonial language is already the property of a small educated class, often urban and often wealthy, and keeping it as the language of power entrenches that class's position against the rural majority of every linguistic group. The choice, then, is not between authenticity and convenience but between two kinds of inequality: one that runs between language communities, and one that runs between classes within each of them. Recognising this does not settle what any particular country should do, and it is not an argument for pretending the dilemma away. It does suggest that the sharpest debates about language after empire have rarely been about nostalgia or national pride, whatever their rhetoric. They have been about who will be able to read the forms, pass the examinations and understand the judge. Policies that use several languages at different levels of government, though cumbersome, are best understood as attempts to spread these costs rather than to escape them.
R04-B-05: Few images of empire are as familiar as that of European diplomats bent over a map of Africa, ruler in hand, dividing a continent they had barely visited. The image is usually summoned to explain why so many of the continent's borders run in straight lines, and why so many of its states have struggled: the borders, it is said, were artificial, cutting across peoples and lumping together others who had nothing in common, and the conflicts of the post-colonial era are their bitter harvest. The story has the merit of placing responsibility where much of it belongs. As an explanation, however, it is weaker than its popularity suggests. Begin with the image itself. The conference held in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 is often remembered as the moment of partition, but it chiefly agreed on rules by which European powers would recognise one another's claims. Most actual boundaries were settled afterwards, over decades, through bilateral treaties, exchanges of territory and survey commissions, and many of them followed rivers, watersheds or the limits of existing polities rather than lines of latitude. The straight lines are real, but they cluster in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people. More fundamentally, the charge of artificiality proves too much. Every border is artificial in the sense that people drew it, and many of the borders of Europe were fixed by wars, dynastic marriages and peace conferences no more attentive to local wishes than any colonial commission. If artificial borders caused instability by themselves, much of the world would be permanently at war. Nor is it obvious what a natural border would be. Peoples overlap, migrate and intermarry; a line that united one group would divide another. When African states gained independence, their leaders, aware of these difficulties, chose through the Organisation of African Unity to accept the boundaries they had inherited rather than reopen them, judging that an attempt to redraw them would be more dangerous than living with them. None of this acquits the colonial powers. Boundaries were indeed drawn without consulting the people they affected, and some did separate communities from their pastures, markets and kin. But the more serious legacy lay inside the lines rather than in their placement: states built for extraction, with administrations designed to collect revenue and keep order rather than to represent, and with ethnic categories hardened by colonial policy into the main currency of politics. To blame the shape of the map is to look at the frame and miss the picture.
R04-B-06: Indirect rule was presented by its architects as an act of restraint. Rather than replace the institutions of the peoples it governed, the colonial state would work through them: chiefs would keep their offices, customary courts would apply customary law, and the colonial officer would advise rather than command. The policy, most closely associated with British administration in Nigeria and later extended across much of British Africa, was cheaper than direct administration, and its defenders also claimed for it a moral advantage. It would let colonised peoples develop along their own lines instead of being turned into imitation Europeans. The difficulty was that the institutions indirect rule claimed to preserve rarely existed in the form it required. The policy needed a chief: one identifiable person in each locality who could collect tax, supply labour and answer for order. Where centralised kingdoms existed, such a figure could be found. Where authority had been spread among councils of elders, age-grades and religious associations, as in parts of south-eastern Nigeria, officials appointed men to the role, and the so-called warrant chiefs they created had little standing in local tradition. Even where genuine rulers existed, their position changed. A king who had once had to keep the support of title-holders and rivals, and who faced the threat that subjects might desert him, now had the backing of a colonial army, and the checks that had limited him lost much of their force. Customary law underwent a similar transformation. To be applied in courts, custom had to be written down, and the people asked to state it were usually senior men with an interest in the answer. Rules about land, marriage and inheritance that had been flexible and contested were recorded as fixed, and frequently in the form most favourable to elders against juniors and men against women. Custom that had changed with circumstances became a code that could be changed only by the administration. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that tradition was simply invented by colonial officials and imposed on passive subjects. The elders who told officers what the custom was were pursuing their own ends, and they often succeeded; the codes bear their fingerprints as much as the administrators'. That is precisely what makes indirect rule instructive. Its most lasting effect was not the preservation of old authority, nor its outright replacement, but the creation of a new kind of authority that spoke the language of tradition while answering upward to the state rather than downward to the governed. Many post-colonial governments, finding such authority convenient, kept it.
R04-B-07: The doctrine that a territory could be treated as belonging to no one, terra nullius, is often described as a lie that settlers told themselves. The lands of Australia or North America, the argument runs, were plainly inhabited; to declare them empty was either a culpable ignorance or a convenient fiction, and once the facts are acknowledged the doctrine collapses. There is something right in this, but it misdescribes the doctrine's real strength. Most of the people who invoked the idea of empty land were perfectly aware that others lived there. What they denied was not presence but a particular kind of relationship to the land, one that their own law was prepared to recognise as ownership. The intellectual resources for that denial were readily available. An influential strand of early modern European thought held that property arose when a person mixed his labour with the earth, enclosing it, ploughing it and improving it; John Locke's well-known version of the argument drew explicitly on the example of America. On this view, land that was hunted over, gathered from, burned to renew its grasses or moved across with the seasons had not yet been appropriated, however long people had lived on it. The settlers' error, if it was one, was not a failure to see but a theory of what was worth seeing. Fences, fields and permanent buildings registered as use; songs that mapped water sources, rules governing who might hunt where, and the careful management of fire did not. This matters because the doctrine has now been formally repudiated in several places, most famously when the High Court of Australia in 1992 rejected the proposition that the continent had belonged to no one at the time of British settlement, a proposition on which much of the country's land law had quietly rested. The repudiation was a real achievement, and it would be ungracious to belittle it. Yet the regimes of native title that followed typically require claimants to show that they have maintained a continuing connection with the land under traditional laws and customs, often to the satisfaction of courts that weigh written records and documented occupation heavily. Communities that were driven off their country, or whose practices were suppressed, find that the very dispossession they complain of becomes evidence against them: a broken connection, however it was broken, is a weaker claim. In other words, the factual premise of terra nullius has been abandoned while something like its theoretical premise survives. Title still depends on displaying a relationship to land in forms that a court is equipped to recognise, and the forms most easily recognised are those that leave records. The burden has simply been reversed. Where the settler state once declared the land empty and left the inhabitants to prove otherwise in practice, the modern claimant must now prove, in a forum designed by the settler state, that the land was never emptied of them. It does not follow that recognition is worthless, or that some purer form of restitution is readily available. Any legal system must have rules of proof, and claims that could be made without evidence would invite abuse. The point is narrower. A doctrine is not fully dismantled when its conclusion is reversed if the standard used to apply the reversal was shaped by the doctrine itself. To finish the work would require asking not only whether people were present, which no one now denies, but whose ways of being present count as having a place.
R04-B-08: The end of empire is usually pictured as a ceremony. A flag is lowered at midnight, another is raised, a governor boards a ship, and a new state takes its seat in the international order. Historians have long known that the picture is too tidy, and a powerful critique, voiced by some of the leaders of newly independent states themselves and given the name neo-colonialism, holds that it is not merely tidy but false. On this account, formal independence changed the personnel and the symbols of rule while leaving its substance intact: the new states still sold raw materials at prices set elsewhere, borrowed from foreign banks, bought foreign manufactures and relied on foreign advisers. The flag changed; the economy did not. The critique captured something the ceremonial picture ignores, and it remains a useful corrective to triumphal accounts. Yet it shares more with the view it attacks than either side usually admits. Both treat empire as a single thing that either ends or persists, so that the only question is whether the moment of independence marked its end. Empire was not a single thing. It was a bundle of relations, held together by the power of the imperial state: sovereignty over territory and law, control of trade and currency, the organisation of armed force, the training of an administrative and professional class, the language in which public life was conducted, and the habits of deference and aspiration that all these produced. There is no reason to expect such strands to have come apart at the same speed, and they did not. Sovereignty, the strand that the ceremony marked, ended at a stroke, and its ending was not trivial. A sovereign government could nationalise a foreign-owned mine, change its alliances, write a new constitution, expel a foreign base or make ruinous mistakes of its own, and many did each of these things. Other strands loosened over decades. Monetary arrangements tying several former colonies' currencies to that of the former ruler persisted long after independence; legal systems, curricula and civil-service procedures inherited from the colonial period often outlasted the governments that had installed them; the former metropolis remained, for many, the place where one went to study and to be taken seriously. Some of these continuities were imposed through unequal bargaining at the moment of transfer. Others were chosen, and defended, by new elites who had been formed by the old system and found its institutions congenial. Seen as an unbundling, decolonisation ceases to be an event that either happened or did not, and becomes a set of processes whose timing differed by strand and by place. This has a practical as well as a historiographical consequence. The question 'When did empire end?' admits no good answer, and debates conducted in its terms tend to stall, with one side pointing to the ceremonies and the other to the trade figures. The better question is which relations were transformed, when, by whom and at what cost. It allows one to say, without contradiction, that a country became fully sovereign in a given year and that its banking system or its universities remained oriented toward its former ruler for a generation. It also places responsibility more precisely. If the persistence of colonial patterns were simply the continuation of empire by other means, then the governments of independent states would be its passive victims. If some strands were retained by choice, those governments must answer for the choosing, just as former imperial powers must answer for the strands they kept by pressure. The unbundled view is less satisfying than either of the stories it replaces, since it yields no single date and no single villain. That is not a weakness in a historical account; it is usually a sign that the account has begun to fit its subject.
